tx.t: Today I would like to talk about the Silk Road, one of the greatest trade networks in history. It was not a single road but a network of routes connecting China with the Mediterranean.
The main routes were more than six thousand kilometres long. The Chinese envoy Zhang Qian travelled west around one hundred and thirty BC and helped to open the routes.

Cities such as Samarkand and Bukhara, in what is now Uzbekistan, became rich and famous centres of trade. Besides silk, merchants carried spices, paper, glass and precious stones, and also ideas and religions.
The routes became less important when sea trade grew cheaper in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries.

tx.t: Today I want to explain why sleep is so important, and what happens in the brain during the night. Adults need between seven and nine hours of sleep a night, while teenagers need eight to ten.

A full cycle of sleep lasts about ninety minutes, and we go through four or five cycles each night. Most vivid dreams happen during a stage called REM sleep, when the eyes move quickly under the eyelids.

While we sleep, the brain moves memories from short-term storage into long-term storage. Lack of sleep makes it harder to concentrate and slows reaction times, which is why tired drivers cause many accidents.
On average, people spend about one third of their lives asleep.

tx.t: In this lecture I will describe the Aral Sea, one of the biggest environmental disasters of the last century. The Aral Sea, between Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan, was once the fourth largest lake in the world.

From the nineteen sixties, water from the two rivers that fed it, the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya, was taken to irrigate cotton fields. By two thousand and seven, the sea had lost about ninety per cent of its volume.
The fishing industry collapsed, and ships were left on dry sand near the town of Moynaq. The exposed seabed is now a desert called the Aralkum, where salty dust storms harm people's health.
Today, tree planting on the old seabed and a dam in the northern part have helped to restore some of the water.

tx.t: In this talk I will explain what psychologists know about memory and how students can use it. In eighteen eighty-five, the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus described the forgetting curve.
He found that people forget roughly half of new material within an hour if they do not review it. In nineteen fifty-six, George Miller suggested that short-term memory holds about seven items.
Reviewing material at increasing intervals, which is called spaced repetition, helps to move it into long-term memory. Testing yourself is more effective than simply reading your notes again.
A good night of sleep after studying helps to store what you have learned.

tx.t: This lecture is about a successful conservation project in the Harwood Hills. In nineteen eighty-two, only thirty-four pairs of red squirrels were counted there.
The main reason for the decline was disturbance from walkers and dogs. So volunteers and rangers created protected zones with quiet paths.
By twenty twenty, the number had risen to four hundred and eleven pairs, which shows that careful management can work.
